hashing-python-functions::1.title: Working with Python *where*-functions
hashing-python-functions::1.snippetHtml:
For the past two years, I've developed my machine learning projects with JAX and Equinox. The basis of JAX's power is how flexibly we can compose our computation graphs by writing in a functional paradigm, using transformations like grad, vmap, and jit. But the substance of its power is PyTrees, or the ability to transform over arbitrary types of tree-structured inputs in a unified way.

To be clear: "a PyTree" is code for "some nested composition of nodes, which JAX knows how to treat like any other tree because it's been told how to flatten and unflatten the nodes". Technically every Python object is a PyTree, even if it is treated as just a single leaf.

hashing-python-functions::3.title: Working with Python *where*-functions
hashing-python-functions::3.snippetHtml: Where-functions are just functions which access one or more nodes from an input PyTree: they return a different PyTree, composed of one or more nodes from the input.

from collections.abc import Callable
from jaxtyping import Array, PyTree

def replace_nodes(tree: PyTree, spec: Sequence[tuple[Callable, Any]]):
    for where_func, node_value in spec:
        tree = eqx.tree_at(where_func, tree, node_value)
    return tree
```

Perhaps it is better to assume in this case that our where-functions will specify individual, unique leaves (or at least, trees of non-intersecting subsets of leaves). So, suppose instead we use the function:

hashing-python-functions::29.title: Working with Python *where*-functions
hashing-python-functions::29.snippetHtml: At first this might seem kind of weird. Not only is lambda model: model.some_layer obviously identical to lambda model: model.some_layer in how it's written (i.e. its structure, or syntax), but the two are also obviously identical in how we should expect them to behave (i.e. their meaning, or semantics). Actually, in the case of a where-function, syntax and semantics are pretty closely aligned in general: once we know its syntax then we can be pretty certain about what it is going to return, and vice versa, since it's just performing some simple accesses of parts of a data structure.

hashing-python-functions::30.title: Working with Python *where*-functions
hashing-python-functions::30.snippetHtml: If functions were hashed in terms of either syntax or semantics, then our where-functions' uniqueness would be determined in the way we want. Seems pretty useful! So why wouldn't Python evaluate hashes or equivalence, in terms of either syntax or semantics?

hashing-python-functions::31.title: Working with Python *where*-functions
hashing-python-functions::31.snippetHtml: Semantics? That's easy. And by "easy", of course I mean impossible: it's a well-known mathematical fact that there's no general method by which we can test whether any two functions will always behave the same way, for all inputs. So if programming language designers want tools like hash and == operators to be general-purpose, and useful for comparing any two functions their users might write, then those tools can't be based on semantics.

hashing-python-functions::32.title: Working with Python *where*-functions
hashing-python-functions::32.snippetHtml: We could also try to evaluate equivalence in terms of syntax, which is the structure of the function's code. This is at least possible, when we have access to the code. But it could be kind of expensive (ref?). Maybe it's enough most of the time to know that two functions aren't literally identical in memory. Anyway, that's what Python assumes!

hashing-python-functions::33.snippetHtml: Since dict uses hash to determine the uniqueness of keys, and the hash of a where-function is not determined by what it picks out, dict cannot see our where-functions the way we see them.

from collections.abc import Callable
import dis


def get_where_str(where_func: Callable) -> str:
    """
    Returns a string representation of the (nested) attributes accessed by a function.

    Only works for functions that take a single argument, and return that argument,
    or a single (nested) attribute accessed from the argument.
    """
    bytecode = dis.Bytecode(where_func)
    return ".".join(
        instr.argrepr for instr in bytecode 
        if instr.opname == "LOAD_ATTR"
    )
```

from collections.abc import Callable
from operator import attrgetter

from jaxtyping import PyTree


def attr_str_tree_to_where_func(tree: PyTree[str, 'T']) -> Callable[[[PyTree], PyTree[Any, 'T']]:
    """Reverse transformation to `where_func_to_attr_str_tree`.

    Takes a PyTree of strings describing attribute accesses, and returns a function
    that returns a PyTree of attributes.
    """
    getters = jt.map(lambda s: attrgetter(s), tree)

    def where_func(obj):
        return jt.map(lambda g: g(obj), getters)

    return where_func
```

from collections.abc import Callable
from typing import TypeVar

import equinox as eqx
import jax.tree as jt
from jax.tree_util import register_pytree_node_class
from jaxtyping import Array, PyTree


T = TypeVar('T')


def _where_to_str(where: Callable) -> str:
    """Return a single string representing a where-function."""
    terms = where_func_to_attr_str_tree(where)
    if isinstance(terms, str):
        where_str = terms
    else:
        where_str = ", ".join(jt.leaves(terms))
    return where_str

@register_pytree_node_class
class WhereDict(AbstractTransformedOrderedDict[str, Callable[[PyTree], Any], T]):
    """An `OrderedDict` that allows use of where-functions as keys.

    In particular, keys can be callables (functions/lambdas) that take a single argument,
    and return a PyTree of leaves, as visited by attribute/item accesses.

    Functions are parsed to strings, which can be used interchangeably as keys. 
    For example, the following return the same value when `init_spec` is a `WhereDict`:

    > init_spec[lambda state: state.mechanics.effector]
    > init_spec['mechanics.effector']  

    Finally, a `tuple[Callable, str]` may also be provided as a key, for cases where
    different unique entries must be included for the same callable. For example,
    the following are equivalent:

    > init_spec[(lambda state: state.mechanics.effector, "first")]
    > init_spec['mechanics.effector#first']

    Note that the hash symbol `#` is used as a delimiter in the string representation.

    ??? Note "Performance"
        For typical initialization mappings (1-10 items) construction is on the order
        of 50x slower than `OrderedDict`. Access is about 2-20x slower, depending
        whether indexed by string or by callable.

        However, we only need to do a single construction and a single access of
        init_spec per batch/evaluation, so performance shouldn't matter too much in
        practice: the added overhead is <50 us/batch, and a batch normally takes
        at least 20,000 us to train.
    """

    def _key_transform(self, key: str | Callable | tuple[Callable, str]) -> str:
        return self.key_transform(key)

    @staticmethod
    def key_transform(key: str | Callable | tuple[Callable, str]) -> str:

        if isinstance(key, str):
            pass
        elif isinstance(key, Callable):
            where_str = _where_to_str(key)
            return where_str
        elif isinstance(key, tuple):
            if not isinstance(key[0], Callable) or not isinstance(key[1], str):
                raise ValueError("Each `WhereDict` key should be supplied as a string, "
                                 "a callable, or a tuple of a callable and a string")
            where_str = _where_to_str(key[0])
            return '#'.join([where_str, key[1]])
        else:
            raise ValueError("Each `WhereDict` key should be supplied as a string, "
                             "a callable, or a tuple of a callable and a string")
        return key

    def __repr__(self):
        return eqx.tree_pformat(self)
```

series-probability-theory-channels::0.title: Channels (Probability Theory)
series-probability-theory-channels::0.snippetHtml: Sometimes, a simple function doesn't seem good enough.

series-probability-theory-channels::1.title: Channels (Probability Theory)
series-probability-theory-channels::1.snippetHtml: Here's one possible function we can draw, going from a set of players to a set of dice rolls.

series-probability-theory-channels::3.title: Channels (Probability Theory)
series-probability-theory-channels::3.snippetHtml: There are other, similar functions we could choose by changing where the arrows end... but any single function like this one can only give us a single outcome for each player.

series-probability-theory-channels::4.title: Channels (Probability Theory)
series-probability-theory-channels::4.snippetHtml: As a model of dice rolling, this function is pretty useless! Each time a player rolls, hopefully there's actually a 1/6 (or about 17%) chance of each number turning up, not a 100% chance of just one of them.

series-probability-theory-channels::7.title: Channels (Probability Theory)
series-probability-theory-channels::7.snippetHtml: Let's try writing our diagrams a little differently. Focus just on Max, for a second. He rolls five times: 5, 1, 2, 4, 2.

series-probability-theory-channels::8.title: Channels (Probability Theory)
series-probability-theory-channels::8.snippetHtml: Let's merge all the arrows that arrive at the same place into single arrows. An arrow's thickness represents how frequently we follow it—so the arrow that arrives at 2 is thicker than the others.

series-probability-theory-channels::10.title: Channels (Probability Theory)
series-probability-theory-channels::10.snippetHtml: We can show the same thing using a histogram.

series-probability-theory-channels::12.title: Channels (Probability Theory)
series-probability-theory-channels::12.snippetHtml: Now divide his roll counts by 5—the number of times he rolled. This gives a normalized histogram in terms of the fraction of total rolls that turn up each way.

series-probability-theory-channels::14.title: Channels (Probability Theory)
series-probability-theory-channels::14.snippetHtml: Now that we've normalized the counts, the sum of all the points in the histogram is 1, or 100%.

series-probability-theory-channels::16.title: Channels (Probability Theory)
series-probability-theory-channels::16.snippetHtml: When we've got fractions that sum to one – or percentages that sum to 100% – across a set of outcomes, we have a probability distribution.

series-probability-theory-channels::17.title: Channels (Probability Theory)
series-probability-theory-channels::17.snippetHtml: Our distribution says: given that Max is rolling the dice, there is a 100% chance that one of the six sides will turn up. According to what we've seen, 20% of the time Max arrives at 1, 40% of the time at 2, and so on.

series-probability-theory-channels::18.title: Channels (Probability Theory)
series-probability-theory-channels::18.snippetHtml: Now split up the histogram bars, and arrange them vertically.

series-probability-theory-channels::19.title: Channels (Probability Theory)
series-probability-theory-channels::19.snippetHtml: Of course, five rolls isn't enough to get a good model of six-sided dice! We can't even roll once for every side. But if Max keeps rolling and rolling for a while, and we draw up all his rolls, hopefully we'll end up with something more uniform.

series-probability-theory-channels::21.title: Channels (Probability Theory)
series-probability-theory-channels::21.snippetHtml: Whichever distribution we arrive at, at least we're now in a better position to model dice rolls when the outcome isn't fixed to one value or another.

series-probability-theory-channels::22.title: Channels (Probability Theory)
series-probability-theory-channels::22.snippetHtml: Two classic perspectives on probability are frequentism and Bayesianism.

series-probability-theory-channels::23.title: Channels (Probability Theory)
series-probability-theory-channels::23.snippetHtml: It's rather frequentist of us to build a probability distribution for dice rolls by getting Max to roll the dice over and over while we count the results – and expect that eventually, our percentages will settle on the "true" distribution.

series-probability-theory-channels::24.title: Channels (Probability Theory)
series-probability-theory-channels::24.snippetHtml: The Bayesian perspective is a bit more difficult to explain.

series-probability-theory-channels::25.title: Channels (Probability Theory)
series-probability-theory-channels::25.snippetHtml: Bayesianism does not fixate on experiments that repeat as long as possible and eventually converge on the truth independently of the strength of our prior beliefs.

series-probability-theory-channels::26.title: Channels (Probability Theory)
series-probability-theory-channels::26.snippetHtml: We always start with some knowledge. Often we have an idea of how likely an outcome of some process is, even when we've never sampled that process before.

series-probability-theory-channels::27.title: Channels (Probability Theory)
series-probability-theory-channels::27.snippetHtml: All knowledge is connected. If we know enough about dice manufacturing and classical physics, we may be able to convincingly argue that the probability of rolling each number is about 1/6, without having rolled the dice even once. And even when we can't explicitly support our beliefs on knowledge from other areas of life, our rather huge brains provide us with intuitions that start to become useful well before we've made them explicit.

series-probability-theory-channels::28.title: Channels (Probability Theory)
series-probability-theory-channels::28.snippetHtml: If I'm a Bayesian, I might hold a 1/6 prior belief for any reason at all. It might be hard for me to explain why I hold it, yet. But when my friend hands me dice and I roll 4 five times in a row – according to my prior belief, the chance of that is only about 0.01% – I'll have to start to update my belief to reflect that his dice are probably not fair.

series-probability-theory-channels::29.title: Channels (Probability Theory)
series-probability-theory-channels::29.snippetHtml: From a Bayesian perspective, it isn't that repeated experiments (or significance tests) are useless – they're just one kind of tool we can use to update our beliefs. And they're limited by how they frame our questions: through a repeatable experiment with well-defined outcomes. But to be repeatable, the context in which it makes sense to perform the experiment must itself be predictable. Do we start from predictable, or do we arrive there?

series-probability-theory-channels::30.title: Channels (Probability Theory)
series-probability-theory-channels::30.snippetHtml: Of course, we can still use frequentist tools. In practice, their limitations are manageable when we put enough effort into predicting (or maintaining) the contexts in which it makes sense to perform repeated experiments.

series-probability-theory-channels::32.title: Channels (Probability Theory)
series-probability-theory-channels::32.snippetHtml: To properly model probability, we'll use channels. Here's an abstract example:

series-probability-theory-channels::33.title: Channels (Probability Theory)
series-probability-theory-channels::33.snippetHtml: For each point in the source set, we get an entire distribution on the target, just like we did for Max's dice rolls.

series-probability-theory-channels::34.title: Channels (Probability Theory)
series-probability-theory-channels::34.snippetHtml: Whenever we draw a channel, any arrows that start at the same point will have the same color – and form a distribution. There's two source points in our last example, so there's two (vertical) histograms—one blue, one orange.

series-probability-theory-channels::35.title: Channels (Probability Theory)
series-probability-theory-channels::35.snippetHtml: The bars of different colors grouped under each point in the target don't need to form a distribution. Here's a different channel between the same source and target sets:

series-probability-theory-channels::37.title: Channels (Probability Theory)
series-probability-theory-channels::37.snippetHtml: There's an 85% or a 95% chance that we'll arrive at $y_3$ when we start from $x_1$ or $x_2$, respectively. So the bars under $y_3$ sum to 180%, and of course that doesn't form a distribution. But all three blue bars sum to 100%, as do all three orange.

series-probability-theory-channels::38.title: Channels (Probability Theory)
series-probability-theory-channels::38.snippetHtml: At the start of this series, I said we'd be dealing with functions. Now I've said that we'll be working with channels. But don't channels break the rules of functions? Multiple arrows start at the same place!

series-probability-theory-channels::39.title: Channels (Probability Theory)
series-probability-theory-channels::39.snippetHtml: Well, when we want to get formal about it, a channel really can be seen as a function. It's just not as simple as the functions we've seen so far.

series-probability-theory-channels::40.title: Channels (Probability Theory)
series-probability-theory-channels::40.snippetHtml: A "simple" function looks like $f:X\to Y$, where $X$ and $Y$ are sets of outcomes. This won't work for probability, since for each $x\in X$, we can only reach a single outcome $y\in Y$ with 100% probability.

series-probability-theory-channels::41.title: Channels (Probability Theory)
series-probability-theory-channels::41.snippetHtml: Now, say we also have a fancy function $\mathcalD(\cdot)$ that takes a set, and "expands" it to give us the set of all possible distributions on that set.

series-probability-theory-channels::42.title: Channels (Probability Theory)
series-probability-theory-channels::42.snippetHtml: Then a channel from $X$ to $Y$ is a function $f:X\to \mathcalD(Y)$, which you might also see written $f: X\klarrow Y$. For each point in $X$, $f$ maps it to a single point in $\mathcalD(Y)$, like a function must – but that single point refers to a whole distribution over the points of $Y$.

series-probability-theory-channels::43.title: Channels (Probability Theory)
series-probability-theory-channels::43.snippetHtml: Consider this channel from a two-element source to a two-element target:

series-probability-theory-channels::45.title: Channels (Probability Theory)
series-probability-theory-channels::45.snippetHtml: Here's how we could draw this channel as a function that respects the rules:

series-probability-theory-channels::46.title: Channels (Probability Theory)
series-probability-theory-channels::46.snippetHtml: Probabilities are real numbers. There are infinitely many real numbers. It doesn't matter that our target $Y$ has only two points in this case—we need to assign a real number to each of them, so there's an uncountably infinite number of distributions on our target. We've skipped over most of them in the diagram above, with the help of some dots.

series-probability-theory-channels::47.title: Channels (Probability Theory)
series-probability-theory-channels::47.snippetHtml: There is one other way we could show this in a diagram. For each point (distribution) in $\mathcalD(Y)$ there are two real numbers (probabilities). They must add up to $1$, so we only need to remember one of them – if I know one is 0.6, the other one must of course be 0.4. So we could draw a diagram that maps to just one real number for each point in $X$ – say, the probability of arriving at $y_1$.

series-probability-theory-channels::49.title: Channels (Probability Theory)
series-probability-theory-channels::49.snippetHtml: These two diagrams may be more formally correct than the multi-arrow diagrams we'll use, but I don't think they're as intuitive – and they'll quickly get ugly, when the source and target sets have more than two members.

series-probability-theory-channels::50.title: Channels (Probability Theory)
series-probability-theory-channels::50.snippetHtml: We'll keep breaking the rules, and draw our channels with multiple arrows starting from the same source point. While it's informal and "wrong", visually it'll be nice because it shows how a channel is a collection of hypotheses about how different outcomes lead to each other.

series-probability-theory-channels::51.title: Channels (Probability Theory)
series-probability-theory-channels::51.snippetHtml: Suppose we're asking questions about a specific disease. There's a set $\mathsf{D}$ which has two points: does someone have the disease ($d\mathsf{+}$), or don't they ($d\mathsf{-}$)? And there's another set $\mathsf{T}$, also with two points: does that person test positive for the disease ($t+$), or not ($t-$)?

series-probability-theory-channels::52.title: Channels (Probability Theory)
series-probability-theory-channels::52.snippetHtml: A channel that connects $\mathsfD$ to $\mathsfT$ describes how strongly we believe in the different ways this test can turn out.

series-probability-theory-channels::54.title: Channels (Probability Theory)
series-probability-theory-channels::54.snippetHtml: If the person really has the disease, our channel here says the test will probably be positive—this is the large arrow labeled T pos., for true positive. And that's good, since we want the truth about whether they're infected!

series-probability-theory-channels::55.title: Channels (Probability Theory)
series-probability-theory-channels::55.snippetHtml: But there's some small chance that the test will fail, and tell us falsely that someone with the disease is actually disease-free. That's the false negative case.

series-probability-theory-channels::56.title: Channels (Probability Theory)
series-probability-theory-channels::56.snippetHtml: When someone doesn't actually have the disease, there are also the true negative and false positive arrows.

series-probability-theory-channels::57.title: Channels (Probability Theory)
series-probability-theory-channels::57.snippetHtml: That diagram shows one example of a channel from $\mathsfD$ to $\mathsfT$, with specific probabilities. It describes a pretty good test, that usually gives accurate results. To describe a badly-designed test that usually gives a positive result, even when the disease is absent, we could write a different channel with a thick F pos. arrow.

series-probability-theory-channels::58.title: Channels (Probability Theory)
series-probability-theory-channels::58.snippetHtml: And in a better world, maybe our tests would be perfectly accurate. That'd look like this:

series-probability-theory-channels::60.title: Channels (Probability Theory)
series-probability-theory-channels::60.snippetHtml: We're back to where we started: a channel with all its weight on one arrow per starting point is just a simple function!

series-probability-theory-channels::62.title: Channels (Probability Theory)
series-probability-theory-channels::62.snippetHtml: This isn't a useful model of the way disease tests actually work. Real tests aren't always reliable, just like (sadly) Max doesn't always roll ones.

series-probability-theory-channels::63.title: Channels (Probability Theory)
series-probability-theory-channels::63.snippetHtml: The classic way of writing down a value from a conditional probability distribution uses the $p(\cdot)$ notation.

series-probability-theory-channels::64.title: Channels (Probability Theory)
series-probability-theory-channels::64.snippetHtml: For example, if there's a 90% probability of T pos., we can write $p_{~\mathsf{T}|\mathsf{D}~}(t\mathsf{+}~|~d\mathsf{+})=0.9$, or simply $p(t\mathsf{+}~|~d\mathsf{+})=0.9$.

series-probability-theory-channels::65.title: Channels (Probability Theory)
series-probability-theory-channels::65.snippetHtml: Here's another way we could write this, using functional notation we've already seen: $p(d\mathsf{+}\mapsto t\mathsf{+})=0.9$.

series-probability-theory-channels::67.title: Channels (Probability Theory)
series-probability-theory-channels::67.snippetHtml: Say we have two channels, and the target of the first channel is the same as the source of the second channel.

series-probability-theory-channels::69.title: Channels (Probability Theory)
series-probability-theory-channels::69.snippetHtml: These can be glued together to form a composite that – like a composite of simple functions – forgets what happens in between.

series-probability-theory-channels::70.title: Channels (Probability Theory)
series-probability-theory-channels::70.snippetHtml: The weighted arrows make it easy to see which individual paths are followed often (like $x_2\mapsto y_1 \mapsto z_2$) and which aren't ($x_1\mapsto y_1 \mapsto z_1$).

series-probability-theory-channels::71.title: Channels (Probability Theory)
series-probability-theory-channels::71.snippetHtml: To get the composite, we collapse all the paths that go from one point in the source, to one point in the target. For example, here are the paths that get collapsed to form the arrow $x_1\mapsto z_1$:

series-probability-theory-channels::73.title: Channels (Probability Theory)
series-probability-theory-channels::73.snippetHtml: Even though there's a low chance of following the path $x_1\mapsto y_1 \mapsto z_1$, there's still a decent chance of following the composite arrow $x_1\mapsto z_1$ because we could also have reached $z_1$ through $y_2$ or $y_3$.

series-probability-theory-channels::74.title: Channels (Probability Theory)
series-probability-theory-channels::74.snippetHtml: Paths get collapsed according to this rule: multiply along, then sum across.

series-probability-theory-channels::75.title: Channels (Probability Theory)
series-probability-theory-channels::75.snippetHtml: First, multiply along: if there's a $10%$ chance I'll reach $y_1$ from $x_1$, and then a $20%$ chance I'll reach $z_1$ from $y_1$, then there's only a $10%\times20%=2%$ chance I'll reach $z_1$ from $x_1$.

series-probability-theory-channels::76.title: Channels (Probability Theory)
series-probability-theory-channels::76.snippetHtml: Then sum across: there are actually three paths from $x_1$ to $z_1$. After repeating the multiplication step for each path, we sum the results together.

series-probability-theory-channels::77.title: Channels (Probability Theory)
series-probability-theory-channels::77.snippetHtml: If we have a channel $f:X\to \mathcalD(Y)$ and a channel $g:Y\to \mathcalD(Z)$, their composite is given by

series-probability-theory-channels::79.title: Channels (Probability Theory)
series-probability-theory-channels::79.snippetHtml: A channel gives a distribution on (not just a point in) $Y$ for each point in $X$. So $f(x_1)$ refers to an entire distribution, and $f(x_1)(y_1)$ picks out one probability from that distribution: the probability of reaching $y_1$ given that we started from $x_1$.

series-probability-theory-channels::80.title: Channels (Probability Theory)
series-probability-theory-channels::80.snippetHtml: We use the notation $\ccomp$ instead of $\comp$ to make it clear that we're composing channels $f:X\to\mathcalD(Y)$ and not simple functions $f:X\to Y$.

series-probability-theory-channels::81.title: Channels (Probability Theory)
series-probability-theory-channels::81.snippetHtml: Note that the equation is a sum of products. In our example above, if we label the channels $g$ and $f$, we can write this out as

series-probability-theory-channels::83.title: Channels (Probability Theory)
series-probability-theory-channels::83.snippetHtml: If you've studied linear algebra, this might look familiar: it's the inner (or "dot") product of two vectors.

series-probability-theory-channels::84.title: Channels (Probability Theory)
series-probability-theory-channels::84.snippetHtml: Actually, we can represent our channels as matrices. Then the matrix for the composite channel is obtained by matrix multiplication

series-probability-theory-channels::86.title: Channels (Probability Theory)
series-probability-theory-channels::86.snippetHtml: And our calculation for the single arrow $x_1\mapsto z_1$ corresponds to the product of a single row with a single column.

series-probability-theory-channels::88.title: Channels (Probability Theory)
series-probability-theory-channels::88.snippetHtml: Note that matrix multiplication uses the "last step appears first" ordering, similarly to $g\ccomp f$.

series-probability-theory-channels::89.title: Channels (Probability Theory)
series-probability-theory-channels::89.snippetHtml: In more traditional notation, we could write:

series-probability-theory-channels::91.title: Channels (Probability Theory)
series-probability-theory-channels::91.snippetHtml: The string diagram for channel composition looks essentially identical to that for function composition.

series-probability-theory-channels::93.title: Channels (Probability Theory)
series-probability-theory-channels::93.snippetHtml: When using string diagrams, because they are abstract, it's important to be clear about the type of objects we're working with. On the left hand side of this diagram, are $f$ and $g$ simple functions, or are they channels? In this series, by default the objects shown in our string diagrams will be channels, of which (as we've seen) simple functions are a special case.

series-probability-theory-channels::95.title: Channels (Probability Theory)
series-probability-theory-channels::95.snippetHtml: Last time, we saw that under certain conditions, we can invert a function $\mathsfX\to\mathsfY$ to get a function $\mathsfY\to\mathsfX$. Can we do the same with our channel?

series-probability-theory-channels::96.title: Channels (Probability Theory)
series-probability-theory-channels::96.snippetHtml: It turns out the situation is not as straightforward as it was with simple functions.

series-probability-theory-channels::97.title: Channels (Probability Theory)
series-probability-theory-channels::97.snippetHtml: If there's an $6%$ chance I'll reach $y_1$ from $x_1$, and a $33%$ chance I'll reach $y_1$ from $x_2$, what are the inverted probabilities I'll reach $x_1$ from $y_1$, and $x_2$ from $y_1$?

series-probability-theory-channels::98.title: Channels (Probability Theory)
series-probability-theory-channels::98.snippetHtml: Before we can calculate that, we'll need a little more information. Specifically, we'll need the probability that we had started from each point in $\mathsfX$ in the first place. Our channel doesn't tell us that—it only tells us the probability that we would arrive at a certain point in $\mathsfY$, given that we'd started from a certain point in $\mathsfX$. Consider: if we actually start from $x_1$ $100%$ of the time, and never from $x_2$, does it make sense to say that we'd ever arrive back at $x_2$, once we reverse the arrows?

series-probability-theory-channels::99.title: Channels (Probability Theory)
series-probability-theory-channels::99.snippetHtml: Like with simple functions, we can run into the problem of unfollowed paths when trying to invert channels: when the probability of an arrow is zero, we never follow it – so we can't invert it.

series-probability-theory-channels::100.title: Channels (Probability Theory)
series-probability-theory-channels::100.snippetHtml: Different from a simple function, a channel could reach any target point from any source point. And the only time we absolutely have no information about how to go backwards, is when all of the arrows arriving at a given target point have zero probability.

series-probability-theory-channels::101.title: Channels (Probability Theory)
series-probability-theory-channels::101.snippetHtml: The solution to this problem is called Bayes' theorem, and we'll come back to it in a later post.

series-probability-theory-channels::102.title: Channels (Probability Theory)
series-probability-theory-channels::102.snippetHtml: It will be extremely useful. We already have a channel that tells us how likely we are to test positive or negative for a disease, given that we have it or not. Bayes' theorem will let us invert it, to get a channel that tells us how likely we are to have the disease or not, given that we test positive or negative – which in practice is the information we usually need.

series-probability-theory-channels::104.title: Channels (Probability Theory)
series-probability-theory-channels::104.snippetHtml: The usual way that probability is taught, channels are called conditional probability distributions. Their functional nature is by no means neglected, but it does fade into the background much of the time.

series-probability-theory-channels::105.title: Channels (Probability Theory)
series-probability-theory-channels::105.snippetHtml: On the other hand, it's very common for an experienced researcher to write $p(y~|~x)$ for a value in a conditional distribution, intuitively aware that they're talking about something function-like that starts from values of $\mathsfX$ and reaches distributions over $\mathsfY$.

series-probability-theory-channels::106.title: Channels (Probability Theory)
series-probability-theory-channels::106.snippetHtml: Here, we've kept functions in the foreground since the beginning. Taking this view, channels aren't just one more tool we'll use for probability. They are the atoms of the theory – its moving parts – and almost all of our tools will be special cases of channels and their composition.

series-probability-theory-channels::107.title: Channels (Probability Theory)
series-probability-theory-channels::107.snippetHtml: Next, we'll see two of these special cases – and the fundamentally dual roles they serve.

series-probability-theory-channels::108.title: Channels (Probability Theory)
series-probability-theory-channels::108.snippetHtml: Conditional distributions are also the central feature of the theory of Bayesian networks. Much of what we discuss in this series could be framed as a re-telling of that theory.

series-probability-theory-channels::109.title: Channels (Probability Theory)
series-probability-theory-channels::109.snippetHtml: "Edge" rather than "channel". When we're discussing graph structures formed by multiple channels, it may be convenient to refer to those channels as edges. But in general, I think channel has a clearer flavour of the flow of causality or information.

series-probability-theory-functions::0.title: Functions (Probability Theory)
series-probability-theory-functions::0.snippetHtml: My friends and I are playing a game, and we have a problem. We need to flip a coin, but we haven't got one.

series-probability-theory-functions::1.title: Functions (Probability Theory)
series-probability-theory-functions::1.snippetHtml: There's an app we could use instead – but let's be creative.

series-probability-theory-functions::2.title: Functions (Probability Theory)
series-probability-theory-functions::2.snippetHtml: We do happen to have some six-sided dice. If we come up with the right kind of rule, dice rolls will work like coin tosses.

series-probability-theory-functions::3.title: Functions (Probability Theory)
series-probability-theory-functions::3.snippetHtml: Let's say the numbers 1, 2, and 3 count as $\mathsfheads$, while 4, 5, and 6 count as $\mathsftails$.

series-probability-theory-functions::5.title: Functions (Probability Theory)
series-probability-theory-functions::5.snippetHtml: Other, similar rules would work just as well.

series-probability-theory-functions::7.title: Functions (Probability Theory)
series-probability-theory-functions::7.snippetHtml: Say we stick with one such rule, where half the numbers map to heads, the other half to tails. And our dice rolls are fair: each number from 1 to 6 comes up just as often as each of the others. In that case we'll reach $\mathsfheads$ on half our rolls, and $\mathsftails$ on the other half.

series-probability-theory-functions::8.title: Functions (Probability Theory)
series-probability-theory-functions::8.snippetHtml: We've found a way to use fair dice rolls as a model of fair coin flips.[^7]

series-probability-theory-functions::10.title: Functions (Probability Theory)
series-probability-theory-functions::10.snippetHtml: Our rule that converts dice rolls to coin flips is an example of a function.

series-probability-theory-functions::11.title: Functions (Probability Theory)
series-probability-theory-functions::11.snippetHtml: What makes something a function? Let's get a little more abstract for just a second. Here's a function called $f$ that doesn't have to do with coins, or dice, or anything in particular:

series-probability-theory-functions::13.title: Functions (Probability Theory)
series-probability-theory-functions::13.snippetHtml: A function is just a way to start from one set of things, and reach another set. Here, we start from points in $\mathsfX$ and arrive at points in $\mathsfY$.[^6] The points in $\mathsfX$ can also be called elements or members of $\mathsfX$.

series-probability-theory-functions::14.title: Functions (Probability Theory)
series-probability-theory-functions::14.snippetHtml: No matter where we start in our source, a function must give us only one place to go in our target. In the current example, exactly one arrow needs to start at each of the three points in $\mathsfX$, and end somewhere in $\mathsfY$.

series-probability-theory-functions::15.title: Functions (Probability Theory)
series-probability-theory-functions::15.snippetHtml: We already saw two different functions, that transform fair dice rolls into fair coin tosses. The source set represented the six sides of the dice, so each function had six arrows.

series-probability-theory-functions::16.title: Functions (Probability Theory)
series-probability-theory-functions::16.snippetHtml: A function $f: X\rightarrow Y$ starts from points in the source set $X$, and goes to points in the target set $Y$. We write $f(x)=y$ to say "the function $f$ reaches $y$ when it starts from $x$", or "when given the input data $x$, $f$ transforms it into the output data $y$".

series-probability-theory-functions::17.title: Functions (Probability Theory)
series-probability-theory-functions::17.snippetHtml: Because $f$ is a function, when we write $f:X\rightarrow Y$, we're saying that for every $x\in X$, there is exactly one $y\in Y$ for which $f(x)=y$.

series-probability-theory-functions::18.title: Functions (Probability Theory)
series-probability-theory-functions::18.snippetHtml: In mathematics, the plain arrow "$\rightarrow$" is generally used to indicate the source and target of an entire function, like it is in the notation $f: X\rightarrow Y$. (If you hear a mathematician talking about "an arrow", this is probably the kind of arrow they mean.) This isn't the same kind of arrow as the arrows in our diagrams so far, which start from just one point in $X$ and reach just one point in $Y$.

series-probability-theory-functions::19.title: Functions (Probability Theory)
series-probability-theory-functions::19.snippetHtml: The arrows shown in our mapping diagrams are actually the ones inside a function. These are normally written down like $f: x \mapsto y$, which says the same thing as $f(x)=y$. For example, for the function in the previous mapping diagram:

series-probability-theory-functions::20.title: Functions (Probability Theory)
series-probability-theory-functions::20.snippetHtml: $$f: x_1\mapsto y_1~~~\mathrmor~~~f(x_1)=y_1$$ $$f: x_2\mapsto y_2~~~\mathrmor~~~f(x_2)=y_2$$ $$f: x_3\mapsto y_2~~~\mathrmor~~~f(x_3)=y_3$$

series-probability-theory-functions::21.title: Functions (Probability Theory)
series-probability-theory-functions::21.snippetHtml: Bringing the two kinds of arrows together: when we write $f: X\to Y$, we mean that for every $x\in X$, there is some $y\in Y$ so that $f:x\mapsto y$.

series-probability-theory-functions::22.title: Functions (Probability Theory)
series-probability-theory-functions::22.snippetHtml: String diagrams are a more visual way of writing equations that are just as formal as traditional notation.

series-probability-theory-functions::23.title: Functions (Probability Theory)
series-probability-theory-functions::23.snippetHtml: If we forget about all the arrows inside our function $f:X\to Y$, we could collapse our last mapping diagram down into something like this:

series-probability-theory-functions::25.title: Functions (Probability Theory)
series-probability-theory-functions::25.snippetHtml: The string diagram for $f:X\to Y$ shows the same information, but it emphasizes the function instead of the source and target sets:

series-probability-theory-functions::27.title: Functions (Probability Theory)
series-probability-theory-functions::27.snippetHtml: Note that the arrows have become boxes, and the boxes have become wires.

series-probability-theory-functions::28.title: Functions (Probability Theory)
series-probability-theory-functions::28.snippetHtml: String diagrams are often written bottom-to-top, but we'll write them left-to-right.

series-probability-theory-functions::29.title: Functions (Probability Theory)
series-probability-theory-functions::29.snippetHtml: If the number of arrows doesn't match the size of the source set, it's not a function.

series-probability-theory-functions::31.title: Functions (Probability Theory)
series-probability-theory-functions::31.snippetHtml: These aren't functions. The one on the left has too few arrows – where do we go from $x_3$? The one on the right has too many – if we start at $x_2$, do we go to $y_1$ or $y_2$?

series-probability-theory-functions::32.title: Functions (Probability Theory)
series-probability-theory-functions::32.snippetHtml: Importantly, a function doesn't need to reach everywhere in the target. More than one of its arrows can end in the same place.

series-probability-theory-functions::34.title: Functions (Probability Theory)
series-probability-theory-functions::34.snippetHtml: $\mathsfX$ and $\mathsfY$ aren't the only source and target we could choose. Say we choose a target with three points (like $\mathsfY$) but a source with only two points (unlike $\mathsfX$). In that case, how many ways are there to draw a function?

series-probability-theory-functions::36.title: Functions (Probability Theory)
series-probability-theory-functions::36.snippetHtml: We don't need to label the sets or their points, to show all the ways we can follow the rules. Any time we have a source set with two things in it, no matter what they are, and we want to choose a function that reaches a target set with three things in it, no matter what they are, those are the 9 different mappings – combinations of arrows – we could possibly choose.

series-probability-theory-functions::37.title: Functions (Probability Theory)
series-probability-theory-functions::37.snippetHtml: Say we have a target set with $M$ elements. A function contains one arrow for each element in the source, with $M$ possible choices about where that arrow should reach. So if the source set has two elements, then there's a total of $M\times M$ (or, $M^2$) functions we could choose. And if the source set has $N$ elements, then there are $M^N$ possible functions.

series-probability-theory-functions::38.title: Functions (Probability Theory)
series-probability-theory-functions::38.snippetHtml: Dice have six sides and a coin has two, so there are $2^6=64$ rules we could choose about how to turn dice rolls into coin flips. That also includes the "unfair" rules, though. For example, one of those rules turns all six sides into heads, which is probably not a rule we want to choose if we are trying to model a coin flip. Of the 64 rules we could choose, only $\binom63=20$ of them are fair.

series-probability-theory-functions::39.title: Functions (Probability Theory)
series-probability-theory-functions::39.snippetHtml: Some of those mappings make more sense than others, depending on the meaning we give to the members of the sets we want to map between.

series-probability-theory-functions::41.title: Functions (Probability Theory)
series-probability-theory-functions::41.snippetHtml: The one on the left is clearly more valid, given the usual behaviour of cats and dogs. But what if we choose a different source set with the same size?

series-probability-theory-functions::43.title: Functions (Probability Theory)
series-probability-theory-functions::43.snippetHtml: Humans may be omnivorous in general, but unless you know Max and Claire already, you probably can't say which of these describes their habits better.

series-probability-theory-functions::44.title: Functions (Probability Theory)
series-probability-theory-functions::44.snippetHtml: We can choose any source and any target, and any possible function that goes between them, depending on our purposes. At the start of this post, we wanted to turn a dice roll into a coin flip. In our last two examples, we tried to show something about the diets of some creatures.

series-probability-theory-functions::45.title: Functions (Probability Theory)
series-probability-theory-functions::45.snippetHtml: Once we decide on the sets, the possible ways we can draw arrows only depends on the size of the source and the size of the target.

series-probability-theory-functions::46.title: Functions (Probability Theory)
series-probability-theory-functions::46.snippetHtml: Our comparison between the diagrams for $\mathsfcats$-$\mathsfdogs$ versus $\mathsfMax$-$\mathsfClaire$ is an example of a difference between syntax and semantics.

series-probability-theory-functions::47.title: Functions (Probability Theory)
series-probability-theory-functions::47.snippetHtml: Roughly speaking, syntax is the way we write things down. In terms of arrows, the two diagrams the written the same way. However, the meaning or semantics of the two diagrams is clearly different.

series-probability-theory-functions::48.title: Functions (Probability Theory)
series-probability-theory-functions::48.snippetHtml: Of course, people don't usually draw diagrams just because they want to remember things about people, or make rules about games. But as we move forward in this series, drawing diagrams like these will help us to understand probability in terms of following paths between collections of possibilities.

series-probability-theory-functions::50.title: Functions (Probability Theory)
series-probability-theory-functions::50.snippetHtml: Why do my friends and I need to flip a coin for our game?

series-probability-theory-functions::51.title: Functions (Probability Theory)
series-probability-theory-functions::51.snippetHtml: Because the next player only gets to move if it comes up heads!

series-probability-theory-functions::52.title: Functions (Probability Theory)

series-probability-theory-functions::53.title: Functions (Probability Theory)
series-probability-theory-functions::53.snippetHtml: This is also a function, and it fits together with our function from earlier.

series-probability-theory-functions::55.title: Functions (Probability Theory)
series-probability-theory-functions::55.snippetHtml: Actually, if all we care about is starting with a dice roll and deciding whether the next player moves or not, we can forget coins were ever involved.

series-probability-theory-functions::57.title: Functions (Probability Theory)
series-probability-theory-functions::57.snippetHtml: Gluing together functions like this is called composition. It always gives another function, called the composite. The source of the composite is the source of the first function, and the target is the target of the second function.

series-probability-theory-functions::58.title: Functions (Probability Theory)
series-probability-theory-functions::58.snippetHtml: Each arrow in the composite is formed by collapsing a path made from two arrows from the original functions.

series-probability-theory-functions::60.title: Functions (Probability Theory)
series-probability-theory-functions::60.snippetHtml: The composite doesn't care about what happens in between: the target of the first function, which is the source of the second function, which in this case is the set with $\mathsfheads$ and $\mathsftails$ in it. The composite forgets what happens in between.

series-probability-theory-functions::61.title: Functions (Probability Theory)
series-probability-theory-functions::61.snippetHtml: Given a function $f:X\rightarrow Y$ and a function $g:Y\rightarrow Z$, their composite is $g\circ f:X\rightarrow Z$.

series-probability-theory-functions::62.title: Functions (Probability Theory)
series-probability-theory-functions::62.snippetHtml: For example, if $f(x_1)=y_1$ and $g(y_1)=z_2$, then $(g\circ f)(x_1)=z_2$. That is:

series-probability-theory-functions::69.title: Functions (Probability Theory)
series-probability-theory-functions::69.snippetHtml: Since $g\circ f$ is just like applying $f$ and then applying $g$, we can also write $(g\circ f)(x_1)=g(f(x_1))=z_2$, where $f(x_1)$ is the result of $f$ that gets fed to $g$.

series-probability-theory-functions::70.title: Functions (Probability Theory)
series-probability-theory-functions::70.snippetHtml: This notation might seem weird. We know $g$ is applied after $f$. If we drew one of our diagrams, $g$ would appear on the right (orange arrows). However, in $g\circ f$ it appears on the left! This reversal is related to the notation $g(f(\cdot))$.

series-probability-theory-functions::71.title: Functions (Probability Theory)
series-probability-theory-functions::71.snippetHtml: To maintain the order seen in our diagrams, we could use the alternate notation $f\compo g: X\rightarrow Z$, where $f\compo g \coloneqq g\circ f$. (The symbol "$\coloneqq$" means "these things are equal by definition, and not as a result of something else".)

series-probability-theory-functions::72.title: Functions (Probability Theory)
series-probability-theory-functions::72.snippetHtml: In string diagrams, we can simply join functions together as we would in our mapping diagrams.

series-probability-theory-functions::74.title: Functions (Probability Theory)
series-probability-theory-functions::74.snippetHtml: This is an actual mathematical equation! It says "if we input any $x\in X$ into $f$, then take the output of $f$ and pass it to $g$, then the output of $g$ will be identical to the output of the composite $g\circ f$ if we input the same $x$ into it as we did to $f$".

series-probability-theory-functions::75.title: Functions (Probability Theory)
series-probability-theory-functions::75.snippetHtml: This particular diagram is a valid way to describe the composition of any function $f:X\to Y$ with any function $g:Y\to Z$. If we have a specific $f$ and $g$ in mind, we'll have to say so – a string diagram is more abstract, and doesn't show the internal arrows of functions like a mapping diagram would.

series-probability-theory-functions::76.title: Functions (Probability Theory)
series-probability-theory-functions::76.snippetHtml: Sometimes, we'll omit the wire labels when the context is clear.

series-probability-theory-functions::78.title: Functions (Probability Theory)
series-probability-theory-functions::78.snippetHtml: We use "$\rightsquigarrow$" in our mapping diagrams to say "we can rewrite this diagram, in this way".

series-probability-theory-functions::79.title: Functions (Probability Theory)
series-probability-theory-functions::79.snippetHtml: Technically this is different than saying that the two sides of the diagram are equal, like we do when we use "$=$" in a string diagram equation. As mentioned in the preceding box, when two string diagrams are equal that means they represent the same computation.

series-probability-theory-functions::80.title: Functions (Probability Theory)
series-probability-theory-functions::80.snippetHtml: If this distinction doesn't make sense, don't worry. Just consider that mapping diagrams are a less formal way we can use to write (and re-write) specific examples, while string diagrams are a more formal and general way of describing the computations involved.

series-probability-theory-functions::82.title: Functions (Probability Theory)
series-probability-theory-functions::82.snippetHtml: There's one more thing we should explore in this post. What does it mean to remember the path you followed—how you arrived where you did?

series-probability-theory-functions::83.title: Functions (Probability Theory)
series-probability-theory-functions::83.snippetHtml: We've seen that a function doesn't need to reach every point in its target—but some functions do. Our dice rolling function is an example: there was always some way to reach either $\mathsfheads$ or $\mathsftails$.

series-probability-theory-functions::85.title: Functions (Probability Theory)
series-probability-theory-functions::85.snippetHtml: Functions like this are called "onto"—they map onto the entire target. But notice something else about this function: multiple arrows end in the same place.

series-probability-theory-functions::86.title: Functions (Probability Theory)
series-probability-theory-functions::86.snippetHtml: A function can have arrows that end in the same place… but some functions don't: each point they reach in their target, they reach only once. These functions are called one-to-one: there's only one point in the source that reaches any one point in the target.

series-probability-theory-functions::87.title: Functions (Probability Theory)
series-probability-theory-functions::87.snippetHtml: Our mapping from cats and dogs to their diets is an example.

series-probability-theory-functions::89.title: Functions (Probability Theory)
series-probability-theory-functions::89.snippetHtml: This function is one-to-one, but it isn't onto: nothing reaches $\mathsfherbivores$.

series-probability-theory-functions::90.title: Functions (Probability Theory)
series-probability-theory-functions::90.snippetHtml: If a function's source is smaller than its target, we know it won't have enough arrows to reach everywhere in the target. It can't be onto. And if a function's target is smaller than its source, then we know it can't be one-to-one—there are more arrows than there are places to go, and some must end in the same place!

series-probability-theory-functions::91.title: Functions (Probability Theory)
series-probability-theory-functions::91.snippetHtml: If a function $f:X\rightarrow Y$ is one-to-one, AKA "injective", that means no two arrows can end in the same place. If one arrow starts at $x_1$ and arrives at $f(x_1)$, and another arrow starts at $x_2$ and arrives at $f(x_2)$, then we know that $f(x_1)\neq f(x_2)$.

series-probability-theory-functions::92.title: Functions (Probability Theory)
series-probability-theory-functions::92.snippetHtml: The rule holds whenever two arrows start at different points in $X$. So $f$ is one-to-one because for every $x_1$ and $x_2$ we could choose from $X$, if $x_1\neq x_2$, then $f(x_1)\neq f(x_2)$.

series-probability-theory-functions::93.title: Functions (Probability Theory)
series-probability-theory-functions::93.snippetHtml: Similarly, if we know that $f$ is one-to-one and we find out that $f(x_1)=f(x_2)$, then $x_1$ and $x_2$ must actually be the same point in $X$, which for whatever reason we've been referring to by different labels.

series-probability-theory-functions::94.title: Functions (Probability Theory)
series-probability-theory-functions::94.snippetHtml: If a function $f: X\rightarrow Y$ is onto, AKA "surjective", that means every point in $Y$ must be reached by some arrow in $X$. In other words, for every $y\in Y$, there exists some $x\in X$ for which $f(x) = y$.

series-probability-theory-functions::95.title: Functions (Probability Theory)
series-probability-theory-functions::95.snippetHtml: A function can be one-to-one, or onto, or both, or neither. We've already seen one that's neither:

series-probability-theory-functions::97.title: Functions (Probability Theory)
series-probability-theory-functions::97.snippetHtml: We don't reach every point in $\mathsfY$, so we're not onto. And two arrows reach the same point, so we're not one-to-one. But since $\mathsfX$ is the same size as $\mathsfY$, at least it is possible to draw a function that is both one-to-one and onto – called an isomorphism.

series-probability-theory-functions::98.title: Functions (Probability Theory)
series-probability-theory-functions::98.snippetHtml: There are six possible isomorphisms from $\mathsfX$ to $\mathsfY$.

series-probability-theory-functions::100.title: Functions (Probability Theory)
series-probability-theory-functions::100.snippetHtml: If our function is an isomorphism, then there's a unique match-up between points in our source and points our target. For each of the six isomorphisms above, it's easy to flip around its arrows to get an inverse function, which goes in the opposite direction.

series-probability-theory-functions::102.title: Functions (Probability Theory)
series-probability-theory-functions::102.snippetHtml: These inverses are also isomorphisms, and they are the only possible isomorphisms that go "backwards" from $\mathsfY$ to $\mathsfX$. And because they represent unique match-ups, we could of course reverse them again to get the blue ones back.[^8]

series-probability-theory-functions::103.title: Functions (Probability Theory)
series-probability-theory-functions::103.snippetHtml: Here's a specific example of an isomorphism: a rule that reverses the order of the numbers on our dice. When we roll a 6, we get a 1, and vice versa.

series-probability-theory-functions::105.title: Functions (Probability Theory)
series-probability-theory-functions::105.snippetHtml: In the last diagram, the set on the right is flipped upside down relative to the one on the left, to make the arrows easier to draw. But the two sets are actually identical. The function and its inverse are reflexive functions: they "reflect" back on the same set they start from.

series-probability-theory-functions::106.title: Functions (Probability Theory)
series-probability-theory-functions::106.snippetHtml: For a reflexive function, the source and the target are the same, so of course they are the same size. That doesn't mean that all reflexive functions are isomorphisms, though. We could easily make a function that takes every dice roll and converts it into a 6.

series-probability-theory-functions::108.title: Functions (Probability Theory)
series-probability-theory-functions::108.snippetHtml: This is obviously not one-to-one, and not onto. It's not an isomorphism, and we can't invert it.

series-probability-theory-functions::109.title: Functions (Probability Theory)
series-probability-theory-functions::109.snippetHtml: If we follow our function, and then its inverse—blue arrow, then orange—we arrive back where we started. We can also follow the inverse first—orange, then blue—and arrive back where we started, on the other side.

series-probability-theory-functions::110.title: Functions (Probability Theory)
series-probability-theory-functions::110.snippetHtml: In either case, an isomorphism never forgets. And functions that aren't isomorphisms are "forgetful", in a sense. How?

series-probability-theory-functions::111.title: Functions (Probability Theory)
series-probability-theory-functions::111.snippetHtml: What if my friends and I have the opposite problem we did yesterday? We have a coin, but no dice. Can we just reverse our function from earlier, and find another function that uses coin flips to get dice rolls?

series-probability-theory-functions::113.title: Functions (Probability Theory)
series-probability-theory-functions::113.snippetHtml: We can't. Look at the squiggly arrows – a function can't map $\mathsfheads$ to 1, 2, and 3 all at once. Our function can only have two arrows, but we need six: we want the possibility of rolling any of the six sides.[^3]

series-probability-theory-functions::114.title: Functions (Probability Theory)
series-probability-theory-functions::114.snippetHtml: If I tell you that I rolled the dice and got $\mathsftails$, you have no way of knowing if I actually rolled a 4, 5, or 6. Because the dice-to-coin function isn't one-to-one, some of its arrows end at the same place, and it forgets where it started. Once we follow a blue arrow, we can't follow an orange arrow back—unlike what we could do with the isomorphism.

series-probability-theory-functions::115.title: Functions (Probability Theory)
series-probability-theory-functions::115.snippetHtml: But just like we could with the isomorphism, we can follow the blue arrows back if we choose some of the orange arrows, and follow them first.

series-probability-theory-functions::117.title: Functions (Probability Theory)
series-probability-theory-functions::117.snippetHtml: We chose to map $\mathsfheads$ to 2, and $\mathsftails$ to 6. That won't be enough to return us to 1, 3, 4, or 5 (red points) if we follow the blue arrows first. But if we follow the orange arrows first, our blue dice-to-coin function does have the two correct arrows to convert 2 and 6 back to their respective coin flips. So while the blue function is an inverse of the orange one, the opposite is not true.

series-probability-theory-functions::118.title: Functions (Probability Theory)
series-probability-theory-functions::118.snippetHtml: Actually, the blue dice-to-coin function can invert any such function we choose that converts a coin flip to a dice roll, so long as it reaches 1, 2, or 3 from $\mathsfheads$, and 4, 5, or 6 from $\mathsftails$ – that is, so long as it respects the overall $\mathsfheads$-$\mathsftails$ split of the blue function.

series-probability-theory-functions::120.title: Functions (Probability Theory)
series-probability-theory-functions::120.snippetHtml: These are all of the possible right inverses of our dice-coin function.

series-probability-theory-functions::121.title: Functions (Probability Theory)
series-probability-theory-functions::121.snippetHtml: If the blue function is $f:X\to Y$ and the orange function is $g:Y\to X$, then notice that for all $y\in Y$ (that is, no matter if we start from $\mathsfheads$ or $\mathsftails$) then $f(g(y))=y$, and we arrive back where we started.

series-probability-theory-functions::122.title: Functions (Probability Theory)
series-probability-theory-functions::122.snippetHtml: However, for some $x\in X$ (specifically 1, 3, 4, and 5), we have $g(f(x))\neq x$.

series-probability-theory-functions::123.title: Functions (Probability Theory)
series-probability-theory-functions::123.snippetHtml: Notice that in the first case, the one where the inverse actually works, the orange function $g$ is on the right: $f(g(x))$. This is just the same backwards writing that we saw when discussing composition earlier.

series-probability-theory-functions::124.title: Functions (Probability Theory)
series-probability-theory-functions::124.snippetHtml: There are 9 functions here. We also saw 9 possible functions from a set of size 2 to a set of size 3 earlier.

series-probability-theory-functions::125.title: Functions (Probability Theory)
series-probability-theory-functions::125.snippetHtml: That's because in both cases, there are only 3 possible places for each arrow to go. Earlier, it was because the target had only 3 points in it. Now, it's because the target is divided into 3 points for heads, and 3 points for tails, which we've colored separately – and each arrow needs to stay on its half of the split!

series-probability-theory-functions::126.title: Functions (Probability Theory)
series-probability-theory-functions::126.snippetHtml: So that's what happens when a function is onto but not one-to-one. What about the opposite?

series-probability-theory-functions::128.title: Functions (Probability Theory)
series-probability-theory-functions::128.snippetHtml: We can easily invert the two existing blue arrows, but we have no idea how to return from somewhere we never arrived ($\mathsfherbivores$).[^4]

series-probability-theory-functions::129.title: Functions (Probability Theory)
series-probability-theory-functions::129.snippetHtml: To invert our function, we have to choose one of the two squiggly arrows to follow. Let's map $\mathsfherbivores$ to $\mathsfClaire$ – an omnivore is kind of a sometimes-herbivore, I guess.

series-probability-theory-functions::131.title: Functions (Probability Theory)
series-probability-theory-functions::131.snippetHtml: The situation is opposite to what we faced when trying to invert our dice-coin function. If we follow the blue arrows first, the inverse we've chosen can return us to the same starting person, but the extra arrow we had to choose will go unfollowed (grey).

series-probability-theory-functions::132.title: Functions (Probability Theory)
series-probability-theory-functions::132.snippetHtml: However, if we follow the orange arrows of our inverse first, $\mathsfherbivores$ and $\mathsfomnivores$ both map to Claire and there's no way for us to return to $\mathsfherbivores$ (red).

series-probability-theory-functions::133.title: Functions (Probability Theory)
series-probability-theory-functions::133.snippetHtml: Here, there are only two possible left inverses: one maps $\mathsfherbivores$ to Claire, like above. The other would map $\mathsfherbivores$ to Max—which seems contradictory with $\mathsfcarnivores$ already mapping to Max, though nothing about the rules of functions alone would stop us from making that choice.

series-probability-theory-functions::134.title: Functions (Probability Theory)
series-probability-theory-functions::134.snippetHtml: Any function that is one-to-one has at least one left inverse, and any function that is onto has at least one right inverse. If a function is both one-to-one and onto it's an isomorphism, and it has only one inverse, which is both the left and the right inverse—called simply "the" inverse.

series-probability-theory-functions::135.title: Functions (Probability Theory)
series-probability-theory-functions::135.snippetHtml: If $g:X\rightarrow Y$ is a one-to-one function with at least one arrow, then there must be a function $h:Y\rightarrow X$ for which $h\comp g = \mathrmid_X$. In other words, if we start in $X$, then follow $g$, then follow $h$, we will arrive back at the same point in $X$ we started from. The composite of the two functions is just $\mathrmid_X$, which takes us from each point in $X$ to the exact same point in $X$. There may be more than one function like $h$ that works this way with $g$, and each one is a left inverse of $g$.

series-probability-theory-functions::136.title: Functions (Probability Theory)
series-probability-theory-functions::136.snippetHtml: If $p: X\rightarrow Y$ is an onto function with at least one arrow, then there must be a function $q:Y\rightarrow X$ for which $p\comp q = \mathrmid_Y$. So the composite will return us to the identical place in $Y$, if we start from $Y$. Each function like $q$ is called a right inverse of $p$.

series-probability-theory-functions::137.title: Functions (Probability Theory)
series-probability-theory-functions::137.snippetHtml: If $f:X\rightarrow Y$ is an isomorphism, then $f^-1: Y \rightarrow X$ is its unique inverse, and we get back to where we started, no matter which side we start on: $f^-1\comp f = \mathrmid_X$ and also $f\comp f^-1 = \mathrmid_Y$.
